Seasonal mixing controls nutrient exchange in restored estuaries

Mina Fielding
18 June 2026

Abstract

We measured nutrient exchange across restored estuary channels during spring tides and neap tides. Replicated observations show that seasonal mixing changes the direction and magnitude of dissolved nitrogen transport. The results connect channel geometry, freshwater inflow, and sediment exchange while distinguishing restored reaches from nearby reference sites.

Introduction

Estuary restoration reconnects tidal channels, but the consequences for nutrient transport vary with seasonal flow. This study compares restored channels with reference reaches using repeated measurements collected under matched tidal conditions.

The analysis treats each reach as a source-owned observation unit. We report the sampling design, measured variables, and comparisons needed to interpret the exchange estimates rather than relying on a summary of linked records.

Methods

Field teams measured dissolved nitrogen at paired channel stations over twelve spring-neap cycles. Flow was recorded at fifteen-minute intervals, and sediment cores were analyzed using the same laboratory protocol for every site and season.

For each reach, net exchange was calculated from discharge and the concentration difference between the channel and adjacent marsh water. Replicate measurements were retained, and uncertainty was estimated by resampling complete tidal cycles.

The reported model is J = Q × (Cchannel − Cmarsh), where J is net nutrient flux, Q is discharge, and C denotes measured concentration.

Results

Restored channels exported more dissolved nitrogen during spring tides than during neap tides. The seasonal contrast remained after accounting for discharge and sediment organic matter, and the reference reaches showed a smaller change over the same observation period.

Mean net nitrogen flux by reach and tidal period
ReachSpring tideNeap tide
Restored4.8 mg N m−2 h−11.9 mg N m−2 h−1
Reference2.2 mg N m−2 h−11.7 mg N m−2 h−1

Across the twelve cycles, the restored-reach spring-tide estimate exceeded the paired reference estimate in ten cycles. Site-level variation remained visible, so the pooled comparison does not imply identical responses at every channel.

Discussion

These measurements indicate that restoration can alter nutrient exchange through interactions between tidal mixing and seasonal freshwater flow. The paired design supports comparison across reaches, while the observed site variation argues for retaining the individual measurements in future monitoring.

Data and analysis code are available in the study data archive. The archive record is part of this article's research resources; site navigation and citation-export controls are not.
